note_sections.t: Clinical reassessment needed due to ongoing prostate-specific antigen elevation after an earlier negative biopsy outcome.

A 61-year-old retired plumber entered the diagnostic pathway in mid-2023 after a prostate-specific antigen reading of 3.5 ng/mL triggered a transrectal biopsy that ultimately returned benign results. Currently residing with his spouse, he experiences only mild lower urinary tract symptoms, registering a score of 4 on the IPSS instrument. His clinical background includes chronic kidney disease and Obesity (BMI >30). He is a Current smoker (25 pack-yr) and takes no active medications. Physical activity remains consistent, featuring cycling sessions of roughly 20 kilometres twice weekly, alongside moderate alcohol intake at 12 units per week. Recent visits to a sleep specialist addressed suspected obstructive sleep apnoea, while mechanical lower back pain was managed through six physiotherapy visits; both conditions remain stable. He has opted out of urological research trials and favors a straightforward approach to ongoing clinical observation.

DRE: Normal. The prostate presents as symmetrically enlarged, maintaining a smooth and homogeneous consistency without detectable nodules or asymmetry. Hemodynamic parameters are stable, recording a blood pressure of 114/61 mmHg and a pulse rate of 72 bpm. Systemic assessment reveals no abnormalities, with absent lymphadenopathy and no palpable abdominal masses.
